newsitem.title: USA: Lawsuits, protests greet California initiative.
newsitem.headline: Lawsuits, protests greet California initiative.

text.p: A day after Californians passed an initiative scrapping many state affirmative action programmes, supporters and opponents of the measure filed lawsuits on Wednesday and students took to the streets.

Students held a rally at the University of California, Berkeley, and then marched through city streets, chanting slogans to protest Proposition 209, approved by California voters on Tuesday by a 54-46 percent margin.

In San Francisco, police closed an intersection near San Francisco State University where about 400 students protested the measure. At the University of California at Santa Cruz, up to 200 students blocked entrances to an administration building in a peaceful demonstration against Proposition 209, a university spokesman said.
There were no reports of arrests or injuries.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other civil rights, business and education groups sued to block Proposition 209. They alleged in the suit filed in U.S. District Court in San Francisco that it violated the equal protection and supremacy clauses of the U.S. Constitution.

"No statewide measure in American history has ever come close in scope or effect to Proposition 209's chokehold on state and local government," said Mark Rosenbaum, legal director of the ACLU of Southern California.
No date has yet been set for a court hearing, an ACLU spokeswoman said.

The measure, also known as the California Civil Rights Initiative, bans state and local government affirmative action programmes in public employment, education and contracting in California that are based on race or sex.
The state initiative, the first of its kind, strikes a blow at 30 years of U.S. affirmative action policies aimed at broadening opportunities for women and racial minorities.
Supporters of the initiative also filed suit on Wednesday, seeking an order to force three state agencies to implement Proposition 209 and scrap their affirmative action programmes.

The suit, filed in Sacramento County Superior Court, targets the hiring and contracting practices of the California Community Colleges, the State Lottery Commission and the Department of General Services.

California's Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, who supported Proposition 209, issued an executive order on Wednesday to start bringing state government into compliance with the measure, which amends the state constitution.
Wilson ordered state agencies to send him a list within three weeks of all programmes that would be barred by Proposition 209.
"Beginning today, Californians will be judged by one standard and one standard alone: their individual merit," Wilson said in a statement.

The University of California, which had planned to abolish racial preferences in undergraduate admissions for students entering in the spring of 1998, said it brought forward the new policy because of the passage of Proposition 209. It will now apply to students applying to enroll in the fall of 1997.

The flurry of lawsuits and protests was reminiscent of the uproar that greeted the passage two years ago of a controversial California initiative to cut off services to illegal immigrants. That measure has been tied up in the courts ever since.

Tuesday's vote followed an emotional campaign, with Proposition 209 supporters saying racial and gender preferences discriminated against others who may be better qualified. Opponents said minorities and women still faced discrimination in education and the workplace and affirmative action policies were needed to "level the playing field."
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole supported the measure while President Bill Clinton opposed it.
